candidates.statement: 3.1 Difference between ADR and AE 3 The difference between an ADR and an AE is crucial and yet these terms are widely 4 confused, particularly within the pharmaceutical industry. In practice, determining whether 5 or not a drug is responsible for a particular AE in an individual patient is often difficult and 6 a judgment has to be made. When the judgment of a clinician caring for the patient is that 7 the drug is a possible cause; this should be called a suspected ADR. Reports of such 8 suspicions form the basis of spontaneous ADR reporting schemes. The term ‘AE’ properly 9 should imply that a more systematic data collection process has been used so that events will 10 be included regardless of whether or not anyone believes they might be caused by a drug. 11 So, we use: 12 An ADR: When it is generally accepted that drug X may cause effect Y rather than in relation 13 to individual cases. We qualify the term with ‘possible’ if there is doubt. 14 A Suspected ADR : When a health professional or investigator indicates that a drug may have 15 been responsible for an event in an individual case. A valid case submitted as a spontaneous 16 report to a company or regulatory authority is a suspected ADR by definition. 17 An AE : only in the context of systematic data collection when no element of judgment is 18 involved in determining whether or not a case is counted 19

candidates.statement: 5.3.2 Cohort Study 20 In a cohort study, a population-at-risk for an event of interest is followed over time for 21 the occurrence of that event. Information on exposure status is known throughout the 22 follow-up period for each study participant. A study participant might be exposed to a 23 medicinal product at one time during follow-up, but unexposed at another time point. 24 Since the population exposure during follow-up is known, incidence rates can be 25 calculated. In many cohort studies involving exposure to medicinal product(s), 26 comparison cohorts of interest are selected on the basis of medication use and followed 27 over time. Cohort studies are useful when there is a need to know the incidence rates of 28 adverse events in addition to the relative risks of adverse events. They are also useful for 29 the evaluation of multiple adverse events within the same study. However, it may be 30 difficult to recruit sufficient numbers of patients who are exposed to a product of interest 31

candidates.statement: 6.4 WHO-UMC system for standardised case causality assessment. 2 The WHO-UMC system for standardised case causality assessment has been developed in 3 consultation with the National Centres participating in the Programme for International Drug 4 Monitoring and is meant as a practical tool for the assessment of case reports. It is a combined 5 assessment considering the clinical-pharmacological aspects of the case history and the 6 quality of the documentation of the observation. Since pharmacovigilance is particularly 7 concerned with the detection of unknown and unexpected adverse reactions, other criteria 8 such as previous knowledge and statistical chance play a less prominent role in the system. 9 It is recognised that the semantics of the definitions are critical and that individual judgement 10 may therefore differ. Other algorithms are either very complex or too specific for general 11 use. This method gives guidance to the general arguments which should be used to select one 12 category over another. WHO-UMC causality assessment system considers the following 13 criteria: timing of event; alternative explanations (disease or drugs); response to de-challenge 14 (withdrawal of drug); and response to re-challenge (re-exposure to a drug). Based on the 15 above criteria the ADR can be classified into the following six categories. 16
